Name: phantom_tool_offloading
Title: Phantom Offloading: Do Reasoning Models Think Less When a Tool Is Merely Available But Never Used?
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the cognitive-offloading literature from human decision science, we hypothesize that reasoning LLMs reduce their internal reasoning effort (fewer thinking tokens, shallower verification, lower accuracy) on the exact same problem when merely TOLD a relevant tool (calculator/code interpreter) is available, EVEN WHEN the tool is never actually invoked. This 'phantom offloading' is not justified by any real computation being outsourced and is causally mediated by an offloading/effort-budget representation set at the prompt boundary; steering it removes the disparity.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here. (1) Human cognitive-offloading science shows people offload more as task complexity rises (Offloading Tools in Complex Decision-Making 2023), that offloading is value-based decision-making trading internal effort against tool cost (Cognitive Offloading as Value-Based Decision Making 2023), that offloading causes forgetting of offloaded content (the 'Google effect'), and that offloading can HURT performance yet still be chosen (When Calculators Lie 2019; Offloading Tools 2023). (2) AI work on tool-use decisions reads a meta-cognition/self-assessment signal to decide WHEN to call a tool (MeCo 2025) and studies whether reasoning enhancement amplifies tool hallucination (The Reasoning Trap 2025); efficient-reasoning interpretability reads pre-generation difficulty/effort signals to allocate compute (LLMs Encode Their Failures 2026; Efficiency Steering 2025). Crucially, ALL AI tool work studies decisions about ACTUAL tool invocation and its effect on accuracy/latency; none asks whether the mere BELIEF that a tool is available (with no invocation) changes how much INTERNAL reasoning compute the model spends. And all efficient-reasoning interpretability studies a fixed tool-free setting. We are the first to (a) transfer cognitive offloading to LLMs as a compute-allocation phenomenon triggered by phantom (unused) tool availability, (b) dissociate it from genuine difficulty and from real tool use, (c) show it can degrade accuracy (a Google-effect analog), and (d) locate and causally test an offloading effort-budget representation. This is orthogonal to my prior overthinking proposals, which all assume a neutral tool-free prompt.
Abstract: Human decision science shows that when people believe an external tool (a calculator, a search engine) is available, they invest less internal cognitive effort and sometimes even remember and reason worse. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit an analog: do they think less when a tool is merely available but never used? We construct matched prompts that hold a math or science problem's content and correct answer fixed while varying only a stated affordance ('You may use a calculator/code interpreter' vs. no such statement), and—critically—we analyze only traces in which the model never actually invokes any tool, isolating the effect of belief rather than real offloading. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure internal reasoning-token count, verification behavior, and accuracy per condition, testing via a mixed-effects decomposition whether phantom tool availability reduces reasoning effort independent of true difficulty. Mirroring the human 'Google effect,' we test whether phantom availability degrades accuracy on exactly the problems whose computation would have been offloaded. Mechanistically, we probe whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes an offloading/effort-budget signal dissociable from a true-difficulty probe, localize it via activation patching (patch a tool-available state into a tool-absent context and observe effort drop), and causally steer it to cancel the disparity. A phantom-offloading effect is a safety concern: models silently reasoning less carefully whenever a tool is nominally on the table. We provide an interpretable, training-free fix.
Experiments: 1) Establish phantom offloading (behavioral): For each seed problem (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, GPQA), create content-identical variants differing ONLY in a stated tool affordance: (a) no tool mentioned, (b) 'A calculator is available if you wish', (c) 'A Python code interpreter is available if you wish', plus a placebo control mentioning an irrelevant tool (e.g., 'a dictionary is available'). Generate reasoning traces. CRUCIAL FILTER: detect and exclude any trace where the model actually emits a tool call / code block, keeping only traces where the tool is never used—isolating belief from real offloading. Metrics: internal reasoning-token count, number of self-verification/recheck steps (via lexical cues + reflection-direction classifier), and accuracy per condition. Hypothesis: relevant phantom tool availability reduces reasoning tokens and verification at equal or worse accuracy vs. no-tool and placebo. Report within-problem effect sizes. 2) Dissociation from difficulty: Fit a mixed-effects model of reasoning length (and of accuracy) with random effect for problem identity (true difficulty) and fixed effect for phantom-tool condition; test for a significant condition effect after accounting for problem identity; quantify variance attributable to phantom availability vs difficulty. Control raw prompt-length differences with a length covariate and length-matched phrasings. 3) Google-effect analog (accuracy harm): Split problems by whether their solution is calculation-heavy (offloadable to a calculator) vs. reasoning-heavy. Hypothesis: phantom calculator availability degrades accuracy MORE on calculation-heavy problems (the offloaded computation is under-done internally), a direct transfer of offloading-induced forgetting. Use truncate-and-resume to test whether the model under-computes the offloadable subroutine (e.g., arithmetic errors rise) rather than reasoning less overall. 4) Location — offloading effort probe: At the prompt boundary (last prompt token, before any reasoning token), extract residual-stream activations and train a linear probe to predict internal reasoning length, and separately a classifier for the phantom-tool condition. Test whether, for identical problems, the length-probe prediction drops under phantom availability. Compare to a true-difficulty probe (trained on pass-rate); test separability via principal angles between the offloading direction and the difficulty direction and via predictive gain in a joint model. Layer sweep to localize. Also compare against a MeCo-style meta-cognition probe to test whether phantom availability rides the same 'should-I-use-a-tool' direction or a distinct effort-budget one. 5) Causal intervention — patching: Patch the prompt-boundary residual state from a tool-available variant into the matched tool-absent context (same problem) and measure whether reasoning length drops toward the tool-available level; controls = matched-random-direction patch, off-target accuracy preserved; report sign, dose, specificity. 6) Causal intervention — debiasing steering: Derive an offloading steering direction (difference-of-means between tool-available and tool-absent boundary states) and steer tool-available prompts to cancel the effort reduction (or steer all prompts to a fixed effort target). Metrics: recovery of reasoning length and accuracy on calculation-heavy items, tokens-at-fixed-accuracy, wall-clock; compare to a simple prompt-based fix (removing the affordance statement). 7) Modulators & generalization: vary affordance strength (subtle 'tools available' vs explicit 'the calculator will handle arithmetic'), tool reliability framing ('the tool may be inaccurate' — does distrust restore effort, as in humans?), and difficulty. Transfer probe/steering across datasets and model scales without retraining; test whether RL-tuned agentic models show larger phantom-offloading effects.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences between conditions rather than the affordance per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, and the irrelevant-tool placebo isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. Restricting to never-invoked traces may induce selection bias (problems where the model chooses not to call a tool may differ); we condition on matched problems and report the tool-invocation rate per condition. The effect may be small or absent in models trained to treat tool availability neutrally (a valuable boundary condition). The offloading signal may be inseparable from difficulty or from a generic meta-cognition/tool-decision direction; the separability analysis, patching, and comparison to a MeCo-style probe address this, and overlap would itself be an interesting mechanistic finding. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters, and detecting genuine (vs described-but-not-executed) tool use requires careful parsing; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Effects and their sign may be model-family and scale specific.
